title: What If Lincoln's Guard Had Stayed at His Door?
topic: What if Lincoln's guard had stayed at his door? (Ford's Theatre, 14 April 1865)
mechanism: The one policeman posted at the State Box, John Parker, was reportedly next door in the Star Saloon, so John Wilkes Booth walked up the stairs, showed a card, barred the passage door and fired under the cover of the play's biggest laugh; Andrew Johnson's presidency (pardons, vetoes of the Freedmen's Bureau and Civil Rights bills) followed.

beats.hook: The night Abraham Lincoln was shot, the policeman guarding his door wasn't there: a slow push down the gaslit passage onto an empty wooden chair beside the white box door.
beats.but: Washington, 14 April 1865, the war all but over; a crane over the packed, gaslit house up to the flag-draped State Box where Lincoln rocks beside Mary.
beats.then: His guard, officer John Parker, sits by the door; at intermission he reportedly heads to the saloon next door, where the barman asks 'What'll it be, officer?'; nobody knows if he came back.
beats.conflict: Three days earlier Lincoln backed votes for some Black men, with Booth reportedly in the crowd; just after ten Booth climbs the stairs, shows the footman a card, bars the passage door with a plank and waits for the laugh.
beats.pivot: Now, what if Parker had stayed? In violet what-if light Parker rises from the chair and Booth is turned away; maybe he tries another night.
beats.so: Instead Andrew Johnson stamps PARDON on a stack of papers and VETO on two bills; a balance weighs LINCOLN against CONGRESS as historians disagree.
beats.closing: Parker's neglect charge is stamped DISMISSED; one empty chair in the grey dawn passage, and a country took a different road.

Mary Todd Lincoln: long dark plum dress, dark hair
Officer John Parker: dark navy police frock coat, brown hair, moustache-free
The Star Saloon barman: white shirt, waistcoat, apron
Charles Forbes, the footman: grey livery coat
John Wilkes Booth: black suit, black low hat, dark hair; shown mostly as a backlit silhouette
Harry Hawk as Asa Trenchard: checked country suit, tall light hat
Andrew Johnson: black coat, grey-dark hair, clean-shaven
The house: rows of theatregoers in dark coats and coloured dresses (set dressing)
The White House crowd with lanterns and umbrellas

gags.what: The barman slides a glass down the bar; it stops right at Parker's hand
Booth wedges the plank between the door and the wall and stamps it tight with his heel
The whole house rocks back laughing, hats bobbing, as the actor throws up his arms
Johnson's PARDON stamp slams down again and again on a growing stack of papers

format_note: Illustrative re-enactment: faces and costumes are cartoon approximations. The pine bar and the card are drawn larger than life so they read on a phone. The White House crowd and the lantern light are illustrative of the 11 April evening.
